items.content_html:
Description

Updates the "Pre-render similar primitives or repeating objects on an offscreen canvas" tip in the Optimizing canvas guide: when the pre-rendered image doesn't change, turn it into an ImageBitmap with OffscreenCanvas.transferToImageBitmap() and draw the bitmap instead of the canvas, and call ImageBitmap.close() when it's no longer needed. Also adds a short tip on preparing images ahead of time with createImageBitmap(), including in workers.

Motivation

The guide only suggested drawing an offscreen canvas on every frame. ImageBitmap is made for this: the HTML spec describes it as a bitmap image that "can be painted to a canvas without undue latency", and its content can't change once it's created. As the issue explains, Firefox's accelerated Canvas2D re-sends a source canvas's pixels on every drawImage() call, but uploads an ImageBitmap only once.

The old code example also only created an empty canvas and drew it, so I replaced it with one that pre-renders a shape into an OffscreenCanvas and draws the resulting bitmap.

Additional details

  • ImageBitmap interface: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/imagebitmap-and-animations.html#the-imagebitmap-interface
  • createImageBitmap() steps (the Blob branch reads and decodes in parallel): https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/imagebitmap-and-animations.html#dom-createimagebitmap
  • close(): https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/imagebitmap-and-animations.html#dom-imagebitmap-close
  • transferToImageBitmap() replaces the canvas bitmap with a blank one: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/canvas.html#dom-offscreencanvas-transfertoimagebitmap
  • Firefox bug linked from the issue: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2097484. It's still UNCONFIRMED, so the page doesn't name a browser or give any timings.
  • The transferToImageBitmap() reference page suggests drawing the OffscreenCanvas directly if you only need to copy it once. This tip is about content that's drawn many times, so I left that page as it is.

How I checked it:

  • Ran both code examples in Chrome 158. After transferToImageBitmap(), the bitmap is 64×64, the offscreen canvas is blank, and the bitmap can be drawn more than once. After close(), its size is 0×0 and drawImage() throws InvalidStateError. createImageBitmap() on a fetched Blob worked on the main thread and in a worker, and the bitmap transferred back to the main thread and drew correctly.
  • markdownlint, Prettier, the front-matter linter and cspell pass on the changed file. rari build on the page finds no flaws, and the page renders in the local preview.

Related issues and pull requests

Fixes #46707
items.title: Optimizing canvas: recommend ImageBitmap for pre-rendered images

items.content_html:
Description

Adds a note to Window.devicePixelRatio saying that, in Safari, the matchMedia() pattern the page recommends doesn't detect page zoom changes, and stops detecting display changes once the page is zoomed.

This PR was LLM-generated, but verified by me. Let me know if something is missing/should be updated as I'm not too familiar with contributing to MDN.

Motivation

The page recommends watching (resolution: ${devicePixelRatio}dppx) with matchMedia(), and the live example asks readers to zoom the page. In Safari 26.4+, devicePixelRatio includes page zoom but the resolution media feature doesn't, so:

  • zooming fires no change event;
  • once zoomed, the query never matches on any display, so moving the window between displays stops firing too.

The page's compat table only covers api.Window.devicePixelRatio, which is correctly marked as supported, so readers currently get no warning.

Additional details

  • WebKit bug, with a reproduction: https://webkit.org/b/317839
  • Media Queries 4 says resolution takes page zoom into account: https://drafts.csswg.org/mediaqueries-4/#resolution

Checked: in Safari 27.2 with a 1× and a 2× display, devicePixelRatio was 1.15 and 2.3 at 115% zoom, while the media query resolution stayed at 1dppx and 2dppx. The page's live example didn't log the zoom change, and after zooming it stopped logging display changes.

I'm not sure if there's interest, but we could maybe update the code to account for some Safari edge cases. For example, we could read the window.devicePixelRatio when the window's resize event is triggered to account for zoom. However, we can't account for all edge cases because we can't detect when the window is moved to another screen with a different devicePixelRatio. Let me know if there's interest and I could update the code to account for the first edge case.

Related issues and pull requests

Relates to mdn/browser-compat-data#31282, which records the same behavior as a compat note on css.at-rules.media.resolution.
items.title: Window.devicePixelRatio: note that matchMedia() misses zoom changes in Safari

Description

Split the Safari and Chrome rows of the image table by version, add image/svg+xml, image/avif and image/jxl where they appeared, and fix the Firefox off-by-one ranges in both tables. Add the Chrome 155+ navigation value, which includes image/jxl.

Motivation

Outdated Accept header values.

Additional details

Each boundary comes from the browser source at its release tag.

Chrome (network_utils.cc; request_conversion.cc up to M98)

  • image/avif in M85 (turned on by default): https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/b9d67a157204e822b2140f588f71249ea267f423. On Android it came in M89 (enable_dav1d_decoder = !is_android up to M88).
  • image/svg+xml in M88: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/8997ea79512ef5e4f29773257e4ef44c7b0ee704
  • image/jxl in M155: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/3f500995689490b24355bddb6efdcf76a90ccfb8. The navigation value was captured from Chrome 157.

Safari (CachedResourceRequest.cpp)

  • image/webp in 14: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=211735
  • image/avif in 16, which also moved video/*: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=241904. On macOS 11 and 12 it came in 16.4: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=246925
  • image/jxl in 17: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=254780
  • image/heic in 17: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=257763
  • Lockdown Mode: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=293385

Firefox

  • */* in 47: https://bugzil.la/1249474
  • image/webp in 65: https://bugzil.la/1294490
  • image/avif in 93, not 92 (image.avif.enabled is first true at FIREFOX_93_0_RELEASE): https://bugzil.la/1682995

Description

The vi and vb entries on the <length> reference page and in the viewport units table on the "Numeric data types" guide said these units follow the root element's inline/block axis. They actually follow the writing mode of the element the unit is used on. This PR drops "root" from both pages, and on the <length> page adds one sentence saying the axis comes from that element's writing-mode.

Motivation

On a page where one element has writing-mode: vertical-rl and the root is horizontal, the current wording tells readers vi on that element measures the viewport width. It measures the height. The linked issue has a live example.

Additional details

  • CSS Values 4 editor's draft defines the vi/svi/lvi/dvi and vb/... units as being "in the box's inline axis" / "block axis": https://drafts.csswg.org/css-values-4/#viewport-relative-lengths
  • The draft's changes section says: "Switched *vi and *vb units to resolve against the computed writing mode of the element itself. (Issue 6873)": w3c/csswg-drafts#6873 (comment)

Checked locally: prettier 3.10.1 and markdownlint-cli2 0.24.1 (the versions in package.json) pass on both files. I did not run a full local rari build. I used AI help to prepare this and checked the spec text myself.

Related issues and pull requests

Fixes #46723
items.title: CSS: vi and vb use the element's own writing mode, not the root's

items.content_html:
Description

This PR fills the placeholder sections of the "Data in WebGL" page (varyings, uniforms, buffers, and textures) with explanations and code examples, and fixes the broken attributes example. In detail:

  • Attributes section
    • Fixed the code example, which used vec4() and flatten(). These functions don't exist in plain JavaScript, so the example now uses a Float32Array.
    • Renamed the attribute from vColor to aVertexColor and passed it on through the vColor varying (previously the undeclared fColor), to match the "Using shaders to apply color in WebGL" tutorial.
    • Rewrote the description text: attributes get one value per vertex, and only the vertex shader can declare and read them. Vertex positions were missing from the list of typical uses.
  • Varyings section
    • Added a code example.
    • Rewrote the description text: varyings are declared in both shaders, not only in the vertex shader, and their values are interpolated between the vertices.
  • Uniforms section
    • Added a code example.
    • Rewrote the description text: a uniform has the same value for a single draw call, not for the whole frame.
  • Buffers section
    • Added a code example.
    • Added the missing description text.
  • Textures section
    • Added a code example.
    • Added the missing description text.
  • Added a note that the code examples and terms on this page use GLSL ES 1.00 (WebGL 1), and how the syntax differs in GLSL ES 3.00.

Motivation

The page doesn't state that it's unfinished or a work in progress. It was imported from the old wiki as a draft in 2020, and the draft banner was removed in #10504, but the placeholders stayed. The code example didn't work, and explanations were missing. After the changes in this PR, readers can get a better understanding of the different data types in WebGL and how to use them with shaders. Readers who are interested in more in-depth details can follow the links to other MDN resources on the topic.

Personal motivation

I'm currently taking a university course on advanced web development. I used the MDN documentation for other assignments in that course, so I wanted to give something back to the community.

Additional details

Regarding the note

In the issue, I asked whether a note about the terms that changed in GLSL ES 3.00 is needed. So far, nobody has answered. In my opinion, the note is useful, but I'm happy to change or remove it.

Testing

  • I built a small test page that renders a triangle with a gradient between three vertex colors. It uses the examples from the attributes, varyings, uniforms, and buffers sections and works in Chrome, Edge, and Firefox.
  • A second test page renders a square with a 2×2 texture to check the textures example. It works in Edge.
  • The local preview shows no flaws, and Prettier, markdownlint, and cspell pass.

Sources

Checked against the GLSL ES 1.00 specification (sections 4.1.7 and 4.3.3–4.3.5), the WebGL 1.0 specification (bindBuffer(), vertexAttribPointer(), uniform*()), and, for the note, the GLSL ES 3.00 specification.

Use of AI

I used an AI assistant (Claude) to help translate parts of the text. I reviewed all changes, checked them against the specifications, and tested the examples.

Possible follow-up

The tutorial "Adding 2D content to a WebGL context" says that data can be stored in "varyings or attributes" to be shared with the fragment shader, but attributes are only available in the vertex shader. I could fix this in a separate PR.

Related issues and pull requests

  • Fixes #46631
items.title: Complete the "Data in WebGL" guide

Bumps the npm-dev group with 3 updates in the / directory: cspell, markdownlint-cli2 and parse-diff.

Updates cspell from 10.5.1 to 10.5.2

Release notes

Sourced from cspell's releases.

v10.5.2

Fixes

fix: --gitignore skips nested repositories in ignored folders again (#9648)

Summary

With --gitignore (useGitignore), cspell again skips a git repository kept in a folder that .gitignore excludes, such as a tool's cache of cloned dependencies. Since 10.4.0, these files were checked. A submodule in an ignored folder is still checked, as git does.

Fixes #9645

Before and after

A project with a clone in an ignored cache folder, and a submodule in an ignored vendor/ folder:

project/
  .gitignore     .cache/ and vendor/
  .gitmodules    lists vendor/lib
  README.md
  .cache/dep/    a clone, with its own .git
  vendor/lib/    a submodule

Before, cspell checked the clone:

$ cspell lint --gitignore --dot "**/*.md"
.cache/dep/NOTES.md:1:1 - Unknown word (Thsi) fix: (This)
.cache/dep/NOTES.md:1:9 - Unknown word (misspeled) fix: (misspelled)
vendor/lib/NOTES.md:1:1 - Unknown word (Anothr) fix: (Another)
vendor/lib/NOTES.md:1:8 - Unknown word (typpo) fix: (typo)
CSpell: Files checked: 3, Issues found: 4 in 2 files.

After, it skips the clone and checks the submodule:

$ cspell lint --gitignore --dot "**/*.md"
vendor/lib/NOTES.md:1:1 - Unknown word (Anothr) fix: (Another)
vendor/lib/NOTES.md:1:8 - Unknown word (typpo) fix: (typo)
CSpell: Files checked: 2, Issues found: 2 in 1 file.

What to know:

  • A repository in an ignored folder is skipped with all its files, unless .gitmodules lists it as a submodule.
  • A repository added with plain git add, without a .gitmodules entry, is skipped too.

Description

Explain what 423 Locked means for the requested operation and scope the XML response guidance to WebDAV.

Motivation

APIs such as Microsoft Graph use 423 Locked and document their own response format. Readers should be able to distinguish the status code from WebDAV's XML error format. Microsoft Graph error documentation

Additional details

RFC 4918 describes locked source or destination resources and recommends a precondition or postcondition code in a WebDAV response. RFC 4918, section 11.3

On the pinned Node 24.22.1, all 27 repository tests passed, along with Markdown, front-matter, Prettier and spelling checks for the changed page. The Rari build exited successfully and the generated 423 page contains the updated guidance. The full build reported sitewide content diagnostics.

Related issues and pull requests

Fixes #46692.
items.title: Clarify the response format for HTTP 423 Locked
